abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have been the subject of active research, significantly advancing the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP). From BERT to BLOOM, LLMs have surpassed state-of-the-art results in various natural language tasks such as question answering, summarization, and text generation. Many ongoing efforts are focused on understanding LLMs' capabilities, including their knowledge of the world, syntax, and semantics. However, extending the textual prowess of LLMs to symbolic reasoning has been slow and predominantly focused on tackling problems related to the mathematical field. In this paper, we explore the use of LLMs for automated planning - a branch of AI concerned with the realization of action sequences (plans) to achieve a goal, typically for execution by intelligent agents, autonomous robots, and unmanned vehicles. We introduce Plansformer; an LLM fine-tuned on planning problems and capable of generating plans with favorable behavior in terms of correctness and length with minimal knowledge-engineering efforts. We also demonstrate the adaptability of Plansformer in solving different planning domains with varying complexities, owing to the transfer learning abilities of LLMs. For one configuration of Plansformer, we achieve ~97\% valid plans, out of which ~95\% are optimal for Towers of Hanoi - a puzzle-solving domain.

# PLANSFORMER: GENERATING MULTI-DOMAIN SYMBOLIC PLANS USING TRANSFORMERS Anonymous authors Paper under double-blind review # ABSTRACT Large Language Models (LLMs) have been the subject of active research, significantly advancing the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP). From BERT to BLOOM, LLMs have surpassed state-of-the-art results in various natural language tasks such as question answering, summarization, and text generation. Many ongoing efforts are focused on understanding LLMs' capabilities, including their knowledge of the world, syntax, and semantics. However, extending the textual prowess of LLMs to symbolic reasoning has been slow and predominantly focused on tackling problems related to the mathematical field. In this paper, we explore the use of LLMs for automated planning - a branch of AI concerned with the realization of action sequences (plans) to achieve a goal, typically for execution by intelligent agents, autonomous robots, and unmanned vehicles. We introduce Plansformer; an LLM fine-tuned on planning problems and capable of generating plans with favorable behavior in terms of correctness and length with minimal knowledge-engineering efforts. We also demonstrate the adaptability of Plansformer in solving different planning domains with varying complexities, owing to the transfer learning abilities of LLMs. For one configuration of Plansformer, we achieve $97\%$ valid plans, out of which $95\%$ are optimal for Towers of Hanoi - a puzzle-solving domain. # 1 INTRODUCTION Large Language Models (LLMs), based on the transformer-based (neural) architecture Rogers et al. (2020), have greatly advanced the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP). Their employment has grown dramatically in recent times Li (2022), as researchers develop newer and bigger LLMs. From BERT to the most recent BLOOM, language models have surpassed state-of-the-art results in various natural language tasks. For example, PaLM Chowdhery et al. (2022), achieved breakthrough performance on a plethora of natural language tasks such as inference, question answering, and commonsense reasoning, and outperformed an average human performance on the BIG-bench benchmark. Despite the textual prowess of LLMs, their significance is very limited in the domains that involve symbols. For example, LLMs for domains with symbols such as mathematics Hendrycks et al. (2021b); Cobbe et al. (2021), and coding problems Hendrycks et al. (2021a); Chen et al. (2021) promisingly tell us the failures and deficiency of LLMs when it comes to handling symbols. In Automated Planning, Valmeekam et al. (2022) suggests that even state-of-the-art LLMs cannot reason with symbolic data and offer a new suite of benchmarks to test their reasoning capabilities. LLMs have also been studied to generate code, see, for example, CodeT5 Wang et al. (2021). In this paper, we propose to exploit LLMs trained to generate code and adapt them to generate valid plans. To achieve this, we first create a training and test dataset for several planning domains to support the research in LLM-based automated planning. Then, we present, Plansformer, an LLM trained to generate symbolic plans of high quality in terms of correctness and length. Instead of using a natural language-based pretrained model such as T5, in this study, we use CodeT5 (base), a transformer-based code generation model that achieves state-of-the-art results in CodeXGlue, as the pre-trained LLM due to its ability to generate goal-directed, sequential instruction and semantically meaningful program codes with syntactic and structural constraints. Our experimental tests show that the syntactic/symbolic knowledge learned from different programming languages in the CodeT5 model can be beneficial for the PDDL-based automated planning task. One configuration of Plansformer tested on a puzzle solving domain, Towers of Hanoi - hanoi, was able to generate $97\%$ valid plans, out of which $95\%$ are shortest length plans. This reveals a promising direction to harness LLMs also for symbolic tasks such as planning. In the remainder of the paper, we present preliminaries on planning and language models and then describe, Plansformer, our main contribution. We then present results comparing our approach with off-the-shelf planners and other large language models. Furthermore, we discuss and show the ability of Plansformer to adapt to other domains and brief about the relevance to instruction generation. We conclude with a discussion of the results and presentation of ongoing work. # 2 BACKGROUND # 2.1 AUTOMATED PLANNING An agent solving a planning problem is given the initial and goal states and a set of legal actions, and the objective is to find a sequence of actions that will take it from the initial to the goal state. In this paper, we adopt the Planning Domain Description Language (PDDL) McDermott et al. (1998); Fox & Long (2003) notations. In PDDL, a planning environment is described in terms of objects in the world, predicates that describe relations between these objects, and actions that bring change to the world by manipulating these relations. The output plan consists of a series of time steps, each of which can have one or more instantiated actions with concurrency semantics Ghallab et al. (2004). A planner finds plans by searching in the space of states, where a state is a configuration of the physical objects or partial plans. In the most basic formulation, called classical planning, there is a single agent, the actions have unit cost, take constant time to execute, have deterministic effects, with the fully observable world, domain-specific conditions/constraints and all goals have to be achieved Ghallab et al. (2004). In more sophisticated planning settings, many of these conditions are relaxed - there may be multiple agents, the cost and duration of actions can be non-uniform while its effects can be non-deterministic, the world can be partially observable, and the agent may maximize as many goals as it can achieve in a given time and resource budget. A plan that just achieves the goals is called a satisficing plan while a plan which achieves the goals with minimum cost is called an optimal plan. # 2.2 LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS AND SYMBOLIC TASKS Large Language Models (LLM) such as BERT Wolf et al. (2020), RoBERTa Liu et al. (2019), GPT3 Radford et al. (2019) etc., pretrained on large unstructured knowledge from public data such as Wikipedia, Bookcorpus, Commoncrawl, etc, have shown impressive results in several NLP tasks. It shows the ability to generalize to multiple tasks from question answering and machine translation to story generation and instruction following Wang et al. (2018; 2019). LLMs have shown the ability to adapt to novel tasks with a few samples than learning from scratch Brown et al. (2020); Radford et al.. Most of these works are focused on generating output in natural language. Recent progress in LLMs has demonstrated the generation of structured output that requires precise syntactic/symbolic knowledge with structural constraints such as knowledge graphs Petroni et al. (2019), protein structure Unsal et al. (2022); Ferruz & Höcker (2022), programming languages Ahmad et al. (2021), etc. As the LLMs collect the related knowledge necessary to solve an NLP task, Petroni et al. (2019) have shown that the LLMs are potential representations of the large knowledge bases. In protein data Unsal et al. (2022); Ferruz & Höcker (2022), LLMs generate the functional properties of the proteins by enforcing the structural constraints specific to protein science and determining the complex functional relationships in the protein binding. Code generation has recently become very popular in the LLM research community. Several models such as CodeBERT Feng et al. (2020), Codex Chen et al. (2021), CodeT5 Wang et al. (2021) have shown significant improvement in transfer from pretrained models for natural language to structured codes. One of the key contributors to the success of these LLMs in code generation is due to the fine-tuneup of the models on task-specific data. For instance, CodeXGlue Lu et al. (2021), a benchmark dataset for code understanding and generation with sample codes from several programming languages is used to finetune CodeBERT, CodeT5, etc. In this paper, we use the CodeT5 for further finetuning to the classical automated planning domain due ![](images/ef09bc309261ed295cdbcd14b3b6e3f6004bfbec4031262a95a0b50523cf2aea.jpg) Figure 1: Plansformer Model Architecture showing modeling and evaluation phases. Modeling phase involves finetuning CodeT5 with data from planning domain. Evaluation phase shows both the planner and model testing. to its ability to generate goal-directed, sequential instruction and semantically meaningful program codes with syntactic and structural constraints. The most relevant works to this paper test the ability of LLM to generate symbolic plans Hernandez et al. (2021); Valmeekam et al. (2022); Huang et al. (2022). Hernandez et al. (2021) looks at different ways to generate plans using GPT-3 versions, a prominent generative LLM. Valmeekam et al. (2022) discusses different scenarios for generating plans like finding a satisficing plan or adapting a previous one and discuss encodings to generate plans and verify using a plan validator. Huang et al. (2022) generates step-by-step instructions for an user-defined task using LLM prompting. All these works require the (human-guided) mapping of a natural language-based sequence of instructions generated by the LLM to the admissible action in the planning domain as an additional step. # 3 PLANSFORMER FOR SYMBOLIC PLANS Figure 1 provides an illustrative overview of how we have generated and tested our planner, called Plansformer. The main idea here is to employ an existing LLM and further train it on planning problem instances with corresponding valid plans. We then test if it can generate valid plans (or almost valid plans for unseen planning problem instances). However, the testing consists of two distinct stages: we first test if Plansformer could generate responses as given by the test dataset, and then we test if the generated plans are valid/optimal (independently of whether they were the same plans as in the test dataset). The first phase, which we call the modeling phase, takes care of creating Plansformer from the given LLM. The second phase, evaluation, deals with assessing the competency of Plansformer as a model and as a planner. # 3.1 MODELING PHASE The modeling phase starts by creating a planning-based dataset, which is used for fine-tuning an LLM to generate Plansformer. The top of Figure 1 depicts the different modules employed. ![](images/7a14c06308ddc55cac23eae1cb92bc7def21ec701767cbfe919dfbc65f0acbb4.jpg) Figure 2: Snapshot of one instance of the plan dataset for blockworld domain. # 3.1.1 PLANNING DATASET We create and release a PDDL-based dataset1 which, besides being useful for creating Planformer, can also act as a benchmark to facilitate further research at the intersection of LLMs and automated planning. We make use of the domain model (in PDDL) to automatically generate corresponding valid problem files with varying complexities. In this proof-of-concept study, we focus on four different classical planning domains, i.e., Blocksworld, Towers of Hanoi, Grippers, Driverlog. Blocksworld, or bw, is a well studied domain Gupta & Nau (1991) consisting of blocks placed on a table or arranged in vertical stacks. Here, with the available actions of pick-up, put-down, stack, and unstack, one can alter the arrangement of the blocks. Problems here are generated with configurations of 2 to 5 blocks. Towers of Hanoi, or hn, consists of 3 pegs and multiple disks of varying diameters. Initially, all disks are placed in the first peg, and the end goal is to move the disks to the last peg. The only limitation to consider when moving the disks is that only a smaller disk can be placed on top of a bigger disk. Although the domain has only one action, the problem solving is recursiveGerety & Cull (1986). Problems here are generated with configurations of 2 to 5 disks. Grippers, or $\mathbf{gr}$ domain involves moving balls across rooms using robotic grippers. It has problems generated with configurations of 2 to 5 balls, 3 to 5 robots, and 2 to 4 rooms. Driverlog or dl domain involves moving packages on trucks between locations driven by drivers. It has problems generated with configurations of 1 to 3 drivers, 1 to 3 trucks, 2 to 4 packages, and 3 to 6 locations. With multiple problem instances associated with each domain model, corresponding plans for each problem instance are generated using FastDownward planner Helmert (2006). An input format, which includes both the description of the planning domain and of the problem instance, is coupled with a corresponding valid plan to make a single instance in the dataset. The input format captures all the essential information present in the domain and problem instance, such as the goal, the initial state, and the possible actions that can be taken in that domain. A snapshot of the generated dataset is shown in Figure 2, with more examples in the Supplementary Material. This format considerably reduces the knowledge-engineering efforts required for a traditional planner to generate plans by eliminating the need for explicitly creating two different files - domain and problem. For each domain, the generated dataset consists of 18,000 plans generated for different problem configurations. For training, we use an $80\% -20\%$ split of the generated dataset for each domain. # 3.1.2 TOOLIZER We use a Byte-level BPE tokenizer, following the standard practice in LLMs, with a vocabulary size of 32,005. We add PDDL-specific tokens, namely, [GOAL], [INIT], [ACTION], [PRE], [EFFECT] to represent the goal state, initial state, possible actions with their associated preconditions and effects those actions bring about in the environment respectively. We do not re-train a specific tokenizer for this task from scratch following the suite of Chen et al. (2021), where GPT-3's tokenizer was reused to generate code. # 3.1.3 FINE-TUNING CODET5 With a plethora of LLMs to choose from, we shortlisted the models that have been pre-trained on code to exploit the code syntactic information implicitly captured in their weights. Although Codex Chen et al. (2021), which is built using GPT-3, has reported the best performance in solving code-related tasks, its unavailability to public access drove us to opt for a similar alternative: CodeT5 Wang et al. (2021). CodeT5 is a masked language model, consisting of an encoder-decoder stack inspired by the transformer architecture Vaswani et al. (2017), capable of performing a wide range of code intelligence applications including code understanding and generation tasks. More specifically, CodeT5 can be fine-tuned to perform 4 generation tasks (code summarization, code generation, translation, and refinement) plus 2 understanding tasks (code defect detection and clone detection) on 8 programming languages (Python, Java, JavaScript, PHP, Ruby, Go, C, and C#). Its pre-training tasks include identifier awareness and bimodal generation, which optimizes code-to-code understanding. The CodeT5 model possesses several properties amenable to the planning domain such as its ability to generate goal-directed, sequential instruction and semantically meaningful program codes with syntactic and structural constraints. With this pre-trained knowledge already embedded in CodeT5, we further fine-tuned it with 14400 samples for each independent domain from the planning dataset. As a result of this, the weights of CodeT5 are updated to account for the task of plan generation. We call the model with new weights that can generate symbolic plans as Plansformer. # 3.2 EVALUATION PHASE Plansformer is an LLM that ingests a new problem instance as input and outputs a plan for that problem instance. Therefore, to evaluate its competency, we need to test both its quality as a model and as a planner. The evaluation phase is described in the lower part of Figure 1 showing both testing phases. # 3.2.1 PLANNER TESTING Symbolic plans have much richer information content, inherently captured in their structure as opposed to text. Thus, we have an additional evaluation phase of plan validation to check how well Plansformer can mimic an automated planner. The sequence of actions generated by Plansformer must help an agent to navigate from the initial state to the goal state modeled in the input problem, for the plan to be valid. If the generated plan is also the shortest possible plan, then it is said to be cost-optimal ${}^{2}$ . There are other possible metrics to evaluate a plan, but for this line of work, we consider validity and optimality. The plan generated from Plansformer is passed through a plan validation tool, called VAL Howey et al. (2004), to check for its optimality and validity. VAL is an automatic validation tool for PDDL. VAL takes as input the task posed to Plansformer as well as the corresponding generated plan and applies PDDL-based relaxation conditions to perform a check for validity and optimality. # 3.2.2 MODEL TESTING. LLMs dealing with tasks such as summarization or generation are usually evaluated using metrics such as BLEU and ROUGE, widely used metrics in NLP tasks. In general, BLEU measures precision and helps understand how closely a machine translation (here, plan generated by Plansformer) is compared to a human translation (here, plan generated by an automated planner). ROUGE measures recall, i.e., how many of the words referenced in human summaries appeared in the summaries generated by the machine. In particular, we adopt ROUGE-L, which considers sentence-level structure Table 1: Results of model testing (best performance in bold).

Although ROUGE and BLEU have no direct intuition in Automated Planning, we use these metrics as we look at the task of plan generation using an LLM. These metrics give us an overall idea of the performance of Plansformer as a language model but are not conclusive evidence for deciding how well Plansformer generates the plans. Hence, as described earlier, there is a need for testing Plansformer as a planner. Thus, the initial stage in our evaluation phase is model testing using the metrics mentioned above. # 4 EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS In this section, we present the quantitative and qualitative results obtained using Plansformer to generate symbolic plans for multiple domains of varying complexities. A test-bed of 3600 unique and unseen problems for each domain is selected for testing Plansformer. For all the Plansformer variants, the reported results are obtained by testing on the same training domain, unless specified. For example, Plansformer-bw's results are reported based on the performance obtained on bw test-bed. The two stages mentioned in the evaluation phase checks for finding out the efficiency of Plansformer as a language model and a planner. # 4.1 IS PLANSFORMER A GOOD MODEL? Table 1 presents the model evaluation metrics (ROUGE and BLEU) comparing all the Plansformer models with other LLMs. Actual generations from these various models for various domains are present in the Supplementary Material. In our selection of LLMs for the experiments, we have included best-performing models from masked language models (e.g., T5 Raffel et al. (2020)) and causal language models (e.g., GPT-2 Radford et al. (2019)). The major difference between these two types of LLMs is that masked language models are bidirectional in nature whereas causal language models are unidirectional. Plansformer uses masked language modeling, attending to tokens on either side of the masked word. The results reported are a mean of the model(s) performance on independent planning domains. For Planner, we show the performance on each separate domain as well. Planner performs best on all metrics, followed by Codex, having a considerable ROUGE-L_recall score. Codex's better performance compared to other baseline models can be accounted for by the natural language understanding capabilities inherited from GPT-3 and its ability to generate and understand code. It is also interesting to note that CodeT5, from which Planner is formed, largely underperforms, demonstrating the advantages of the proposed approach. We also conclude that the models pre-trained with code-related tasks have an advantage when it comes to the task of plan generation due to PDDL having some similarities with other programming languages. Planner, although having great performance in the model testing phase, requires to be tested for plan validation in order to see its effectiveness as a planner. # 4.2 IS PLANSFORMER A GOOD PLANNER? The results from the second stage of evaluation where the plan generations are checked for validity, optimality, and the average time taken to solve the test-bed of problems are reported in this section. Table 2 shows the plan validation scores obtained by different models. The considered ground truth Table 2: Results of plan validation

for plan validation is FastDownward Helmert (2006), which is an automated planner. Given a correct input (i.e., a valid combination of domain description and problem instance), an automated planner always generates valid plans. FastDownward is a classical planning system based on a heuristic search. It can generate optimal plans when the landmark-cut heuristic is used within a standard A* search framework Helmert & Domshlak (2011). It can be seen that FastDownward generates $100\%$ valid plans which are also optimal. Plansformer-bw generated $90.04\%$ , out of which $88.44\%$ are optimal and have the highest performance compared to other domains. This better performance is analogous to the fact that bw is the easiest domain among the four domains (although finding optimal plans is hard, any problem has a satisficing solution linear in the number of blocks by putting them down and picking from the table Gupta & Nau (1991)). On a relatively more complex domain, i.e., dl, Plansformer-dl attains $76.56\%$ valid plans, out of which $52.61\%$ are optimal. There is a $20\%$ difference between valid and optimal plans for dl showcasing that the model was able to come up with completely new and valid action sequences, although not optimal. A drop in the number of optimal plans reduces with the increasing complexity of the domains. Both incomplete/wrong generations from the models and failed plans are included when reporting invalid plans. Figure 3 shows an example of incomplete generation and failed plans. All Plansformer models generate $0\%$ incomplete generations for respective domains. It is a testament to Plansformer models' ability to understand and generate valid action sequences for a given domain. The failed plans can be repaired Van Der Krogt & De Weerdt (2005) as they have a complete sequence of actions, out of which some are correct. ![](images/d427ca3050fcc44a436c0e6bede5770532f811822a48a12cd6abdba0ff842aae.jpg) Figure 3: Different types of invalid plans generated by Plansformer on Blocksworld domain (Plansformer-bw). Codex, the second best performing model according to ROUGE and BLEU scores, only generates $0.15\%$ valid plans, emphasizing the need for a two-stage evaluation phase - where both model and generated plans are tested. The average time taken by Plansformer to completely solve the test-bed of problems is 200x faster than the ground truth, offering an immense advantage in generating approximately correct plans in real-time applications. Interestingly, CodeT5, which is used to build Plansformer, takes considerable time to solve the same test-bed. Despite this, Plansformer is faster as it generates valid and likely optimal plans shorter in length than usually long incoherent sequences generated by CodeT5, which tend to be time-consuming. The difference between plans generated by CodeT5 and Plansformer for the same problem is shown in Figure 4. There isn't much prior work to adopt as a baseline and perform a comparison with Plansformer. Although, some recent works such as Huang et al. (2022), make use of LLMs to "plan", it is different from Automated Planning and is not symbolic in nature. These "plans" are step-by-step actions to perform a trivial daily task such as "Apply lotion". These methods make use of a user-constructed prompt to enable an LLM to generate relevant steps from its prior knowledge. The work by Valmeekam et al. (2022) is the closest to ours, still making use of a PDDL-based prompt, to obtain symbolic plans with the help of GPT-3. Their approach of converting the information captured in the PDDL-based domain and problem files to natural language and adding a solved prompt to the problem instance generated $0.6\%$ valid plans, whereas Plansformer, on the same dataset generated $66\%$ valid plans. This enables us to validate the advantage of our approach in generating symbolic plans. Plansformer, trained and tested on the same domain, shows superior performance both as a model and a planner. However, LLMs are also well known for transfer learning, i.e., a model trained for solving one task can be re-purposed to solve other related tasks. Subsequently, we explore how Plansformer trained on one domain can be adapted to another. # CodeT5 b4 b3, put-down b4, unstack b2 b1, unstack x, not clear x, not handempty, ontable, clear, holding x, not x, handempty, ontable x, stack x, not x, not clear x,y, unstack b2 b3, put-down b # Plansformer unstack b4 b3, put-down b4 Figure 4: Long invalid generation from CodeT5 as opposed to a valid optimal plan from Plansformer-bw for the same problem. # 4.3 CAN PLANSFORMER ADAPT TO ANOTHER DOMAIN? The base models, i.e., Planformer-x, where x can bw, hn, gr, and dl, cannot generate valid plans for other domains due to each domain being different from the other in terms of action space, complexity, and solving. For example, Plansformer-bw cannot generate valid plans for the non-training domains - hn, gr, and dl. However, LLMs offer two approaches to enable a model trained in one domain to adapt to another - (a) making use of prompt conditioning and (b) transfer learning using further fine-tuning on the new domain. The model's performance in a new domain in the prior approach depends on a manually identified prompt. A small perturbation to the prompt can significantly affect the model's performance, and creating a perfect prompt requires both understanding of LLMs' inner workings and trial-and-error. In recent times, researchers have started looking at automatic prompt generation Shin et al. (2020), which we would like to explore in the future. We adopted the approach of fine-tuning Plansformer base models with problem instances from other domains to check for the ability to adapt to new domains. Figure 5 shows different Plansformer-bw models and their plan validation scores on respective testing domains. For brevity, we demonstrate variants of Plansformer-bw models on three other domains. Overall, the results for other Plansformer base models convey the same insights as Plansformer-bw and are presented in the Appendix. For fine-tuning Plansformer-bw on a given domain, we have considered varying sizes of problems to see how the performance varies. The model naming convention conveys the information regarding the amount of problems it is fine-tuned on, i.e., bw-hn[500] implies that the base model used is Plansformer-bw further fine-tuned using 500 problems from hn. In Figure 5, we can see an overall increase in the number of valid plans for every testing domain as we increase the fine-tuning data points. Models fine-tuned with 2000, which is $14\%$ of the training size of base models, achieves $50\%$ of the valid plans recorded by Plansformer-hn, Plansformer-gr, and Plansformer-dl. On increasing the fine-tuning samples to that of the training size of base models, we obtain $>90\%$ valid plans for all testing domains, despite their complexity. Plansformer-bw-hn[14400] obtains the best performance among all models, by achieving $97.05\%$ valid plans, out of which $95.22\%$ are optimal. Failed plans keep decreasing with additional fine-tuning data points for all domains. Using the same number of data points as that of training (14,400), the failed plans are lesser than that of the base models built for the respective domains. The number of optimal plans consistently increases with the number of fine-tuning data points for hn and is $13\%$ more than Plansformer-hn, whereas for ![](images/4f6275db551ae06c1ab8b5e407dce31c74f04e202b22eb9f1742dce575865164.jpg) (a) ![](images/22b2a83f1dab7ed5c8eec19dcd4f9f3444dd91c803f1d108eb33cfa11c658202.jpg) (b) ![](images/068afc8628cf5bcc47749a03ead041ce03e3908b56afb51187f1504f8bf14344.jpg) (c) Figure 5: Plansformer-bw as the base model fine-tuned with and tested on (a) hanoi (b) grippers (c) driverlog the other two domains we can see some variations. Fine-tuning results of all possible Plansformer models and their performance are reported in the Supplementary Material. # 5 CONCLUSIONS AND ONGOING WORK In this paper, we have explored the use of LLMs for generating symbolic plans for multiple domains. We have taken an LLM, trained it further over a set of planning problem instances and corresponding valid plans, and tested its capability to generate plans for unseen planning problem instances, evaluating the correctness and length of such plans. We then compared its behavior to an existing state-of-the-art planner, showing that our LLM-based planner, called Plansformer, can solve many more instances with high quality both in terms of correctness and length while needing much less time to generate such plans. We are also working to use Plansformer in combination with an existing symbolic planner in the context of a cognitive architecture inspired by the thinking fast and slow theory Kahneman (2011). In this environment, Plansformer provides complementary capabilities to the classical planner and will be used when resources (time, space, and knowledge) are limited and a small degrade on plan validity can be acceptable. Moreover, the plans generated by the classical planner are used as additional training data for Plansformer. Therefore, Plansformer combined with a symbolic planner constitutes a "learning planner" that over time can exploit more experience. Preliminary results indicate that this approach is promising in terms of the number of solved problem instances attainable within a time limit, plans validity, and plan generation time. Although Plansformer shows promising results, this work is not done and can be extended in many directions. One can seek to eliminate invalid plans comprising both failed or incomplete plans, drive efficiency further, explore more planning domains - e.g., from the International Planning Competition, and tackle other planning settings as identified by Valmeekam et al. (2022). # REFERENCES Wasi Ahmad, Saikat Chakraborty, Baishakhi Ray, and Kai-Wei Chang. Unified pre-training for program understanding and generation.
